title: Chef Kunal Kapur's Roasted Apple Shrikhand Brings a Western Twist to India's Beloved Yogurt Dessert
excerpt: The celebrity chef's recipe combines the warm spices of traditional shrikhand with caramelised roasted apples, offering a fusion dessert that works for both Indian and Western dinner tables.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Chef Kunal Kapur's roasted apple shrikhand fuses Indian and Western dessert traditions.
  • The dish combines cardamom-saffron shrikhand with caramelised cinnamon-spiced apples.
  • Shrikhand is a traditional Indian dessert from Gujarat and Maharashtra, made with strained yogurt.
  • Kapur's recipe reflects a trend of Indian chefs adapting regional desserts for global tastes.
  • The dessert is suitable for both Diwali celebrations and Western fall gatherings.

Chef Kunal Kapur's recipe
  • Celebrity chef Kunal Kapur has shared a recipe for roasted apple shrikhand that combines traditional Indian hung-curd dessert with Western-style caramelised apples
  • The dish blends cardamom and saffron-infused shrikhand with cinnamon-spiced roasted apples
  • Shrikhand, a centuries-old dessert from Gujarat and Maharashtra, is traditionally made from strained yogurt sweetened with sugar and flavoured with cardamom
  • The fusion recipe reflects a broader trend of Indian chefs reimagining regional desserts for global palates

Indian celebrity chef Kunal Kapur has introduced a recipe that brings together two comfort food traditions: the creamy, cardamom-scented shrikhand of western India and the warm, buttery flavours of a classic roasted apple dessert.

The Recipe

Kapur's roasted apple shrikhand starts with the traditional base: thick yogurt (dahi) is hung overnight in muslin cloth to drain all whey, producing the dense, cream-cheese-like curd that forms shrikhand's foundation. This is then sweetened and flavoured with powdered sugar, ground cardamom, a pinch of saffron soaked in warm milk, and a touch of nutmeg.

https://x.com/htlifeandstyle/status/2079501581863788562

The twist comes in the apple component. Kapur roasts apple slices with butter, brown sugar, ground cinnamon, and a splash of vanilla until they caramelise and soften. The warm, spiced apples are then layered over or folded into the chilled shrikhand, creating a temperature and texture contrast — cool, silky yogurt against warm, jammy fruit.

Why It Works

Shrikhand is one of India's oldest desserts, originating in the kitchens of Gujarat and Maharashtra. Traditionally served during festivals and weddings, it relies on the natural tanginess of strained yogurt balanced by sweetness and aromatic spices. The dessert is already a study in simplicity — hung curd, sugar, cardamom — and Kapur's addition of roasted apples doesn't complicate it so much as extend its range.

The cinnamon-apple pairing reads as familiar to Western palates (apple pie, apple crumble), while the cardamom-saffron base remains unmistakably Indian. It's a recipe designed to travel well between cultures — equally at home at a Diwali dinner in Mumbai or a fall gathering in New Jersey.

"Traditionally served during festivals and weddings, it relies on the natural tanginess of strained yogurt balanced by sweetness and aromatic spices."

The Broader Trend

Kapur's recipe is part of a broader movement among Indian chefs to reimagine traditional regional desserts for a global audience. From Gaggan Anand's deconstructed gulab jamun to Vikas Khanna's saffron panna cotta, the approach is the same: respect the original, borrow intelligently from other traditions, and create something that works on both tables.

For diaspora home cooks looking to serve something that bridges both worlds at their next gathering, this one requires no special equipment, no obscure ingredients, and about 30 minutes of active work — plus the overnight yogurt drain.
